PAR: Progress-Aligned Recurrence for Length Generalization in State Tracking

Pan Wang1*   Yihao Hu1*   Guangyuan Dong2*   Yitong Lin1   Hang Wang1   Zimi Liu1   Zhihao Wen1   Jianshe Li1   Jiang-Ming Yang1   Wei Wu1   Yongqi Tong1🖂

1Ant International  2National University of Singapore

Contact: Pan Wang diogenescask@gmail.com

🖂 Corresponding Author: Yongqi Tong yoqitong@gmail.com

††footnotetext: *Equal Contributions.

1 Introduction

Length generalisation asks whether a model trained on short problems can solve longer instances of the same task [1, 7]. Sequential state tracking provides a controlled setting for studying this question: each operation updates a state used by later operations [19]. A rule-table chain, for example, uses each retrieved value to select the next lookup, while object tracking updates the locations of objects after each move [28, 29]. In these tasks, the rules remain unchanged as the sequence grows; the model must apply them correctly over more steps. Throughout this paper, length refers to the number of task operations.

Looped language models offer a way to make computational depth grow with this length. They repeatedly apply a shared transformer block to hidden states, allowing additional computation without generating a text description of each step [5, 9], and can be added to pretrained language models [20]. Iterations have thus been proposed as a scaling axis alongside parameters, improving test-time reasoning [9] and following predictable training trends [22]. On longer problems, however, neither axis helps by itself: on S5S_{5} trained with at most 16 operations, an untied model with four times the core depth and a recurrent model run with more iterations both extrapolate less than 2×2\times, and fixed-depth Qwen2.5 models from 1.5B to 7B stay near chance at 16×16\times (§5.1, §5.2). Prior work demonstrates length generalisation by tying the loop count to task length [7], and shows that intermediate-state supervision can teach a pretrained model to perform successive rule lookups [28]. We build on these results to study how to sustain accurate execution over much longer operation sequences.

A central training choice is what to ask each intermediate loop to predict. A final-answer target does not specify the state after only some operations. On graph reachability, Chen [4] finds that asking for the final answer at every loop encourages early predictions and weakens extrapolation. Intermediate-state targets define progress more directly, but their effectiveness also depends on the recurrence itself. In our state-tracking experiments, such targets without norm anchoring lose accuracy beyond short extrapolation distances (§6.1). We therefore study progress-aligned supervision together with control of the scale of states passed between loops.

We introduce Progress-Aligned Recurrence (PAR) for pretrained language models. At a supervised iteration kk, the prediction is trained to match the state after the first kk operations (Figure 1a). This depth–length correspondence assigns successive task stages to successive loop outputs: on a rule-table chain, for instance, iteration kk predicts the value reached after kk lookups. To control state scale, PAR rescales each token’s recurrent state to its first-iteration root-mean-square norm. The targets specify the intended progress, while norm anchoring fixes state magnitude as the shared block is reused.

The correspondence also guides when to read the answer and how to obtain intermediate targets. A correct answer can deteriorate if the model continues looping after completion (§5.3). We train the existing output layer to predict whether execution is complete, and use a short confirmation window to select the answer without a supplied stopping depth. When intermediate labels are unavailable, we use prefixes that are themselves valid shorter problems. Our prefix self-distillation uses predictions on such prefixes as targets for the corresponding iterations on the full input, learning from final-answer labels alone.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate length generalization in looped models as establishing a depth–length correspondence, identifying state drift and unaligned loop targets as twin failure modes and proposing Progress-Aligned Recurrence (PAR) to couple progress supervision with RMS norm anchoring.

  • •

    We extend PAR with a parameter-free learned halting rule to stop inference autonomously and prefix self-distillation to induce the correspondence without intermediate step labels.

  • •

    We demonstrate 16×16\times extrapolation on swap-S5S_{5} (95.5%95.5\% full-state accuracy vs. 55.7%55.7\% for RLT and 0.8%0.8\% for explicit CoT), show consistent benefits across backbones up to 7B, and isolate the necessity of both components through controlled ablations.

2 Related Work

Looped and recurrent-depth transformers. Weight-sharing across depth originated in Universal Transformers [5], and recurrence can extend computation to harder instances [27, 3]. In language models, recurrent depth has been trained from scratch [9] or retrofitted into pretrained models [20]. Looped architectures can simulate chain of thought [25], exhibit stable scaling behavior [22], share representations across depths [15], and relate to implicit models [26], though depth is frequently underutilized [33]. We address this by defining what each iteration computes.

Length extrapolation and halting. Prior work links loop count to input length [7] or explicit reasoning steps [8]. From-scratch looped models examine stochastic stopping [16], mechanistic limits [18], stability conditions [17], and fast–slow recurrence [30]; among them, RLT [41] achieves strong swap-S5S_{5} performance via token-level feedback. In retrofitted models, per-loop supervision yields modest extrapolation [28], whereas step-wise final-answer supervision impairs compositional generalization [4]. For terminating recurrence, adaptive computation time [10] and PonderNet [2] train halting probabilities with dedicated modules and ponder penalties. Under our correspondence, the existing output head detects completion directly, requiring neither extra parameters nor ponder losses.

Latent reasoning and self-supervision. Coconut [12] and stepwise internalization [6] internalize reasoning along the sequence dimension using chain-of-thought data. In contrast, we compute along depth, using intermediate labels or prefix self-distillation inspired by mean-teacher consistency [31], in the spirit of work that derives training signals from a model’s own outputs, interactions, or environments [38, 35, 34, 13, 42, 32]. While randomized positional encodings improve sequence generalization [24], our positional stretch stabilizes the recurrent step map when scaling to longer contexts without step labels.

3 Depth–Length Correspondence

Figure 2 outlines the PAR framework. We realize the depth–length correspondence by combining retrofitted recurrence with RMS norm anchoring to maintain a stationary step map (§3.1, §3.3), supervising each loop with progress-aligned targets (§3.2), reading completion autonomously via learned halting (§3.4), and extending the supervision to label-free settings through prefix self-distillation (§3.5).

3.1 A retrofitted looped language model

Following McLeish et al. [20], we split the 24 layers of Qwen2.5-0.5B [14] into a prelude PP (layers 1–8), a weight-tied core CC (layers 9–16) and a coda QQ (layers 17–24), as shown in Figure 2a. With static input features e=P⁡(x)e=P(x) and s0=es_{0}=e, the adapter WW projects the concatenated representations into the core, iterating

sk=C(W[e;sk−1]),k=1,…,R,s_{k}=C\!\left(W[e;\,s_{k-1}]\right),\qquad k=1,\dots,R, (1)

and reads an answer yk=Q⁡(sk)y_{k}=Q(s_{k}) from any iteration. The adapter W∈ℝh×2​hW\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times 2h} is initialised to [0|I][0\,|\,I], so with R=1R=1 the retrofitted model initially computes the same function as its parent. All weights are trained, gradients flow through the last 8 iterations, and answers are read with a classification head over the candidate answer tokens at the query position.

3.2 Defining an iteration: progress-aligned targets

Consider a problem whose answer is computed by dd sequential steps (for state tracking, dd moves applied to a state). Let zjz_{j} be the answer after the first jj steps, so zdz_{d} is the final answer. As depicted in Figure 2b, the correspondence asks iteration kk to hold zkz_{k} until the problem is finished. With step size cc (we use c=1c=1), the training loss is

ℒPAR=∑k∈𝒦CE⁡(Q⁡(sk),zmin⁡(c​k,d)),\mathcal{L}_{\text{PAR}}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\operatorname{CE}\!\left(Q(s_{k}),\;z_{\min(ck,\,d)}\right), (2)

where 𝒦\mathcal{K} contains the iterations inside the gradient window. Each iteration must advance the computation by exactly cc steps, so the iterations needed for a problem grow as d/cd/c by construction. Supervising zdz_{d} at every iteration breaks the correspondence: early iterations are asked for an answer they cannot yet compute, and the loss rewards shortcuts that do not scale with dd.

Two depth schedules satisfy Eq. (2). Under forced depth, each batch contains a single depth dd, the model runs R=⌈d/c⌉R=\lceil d/c\rceil iterations, and there is no loss after completion. Under hold, RR is drawn from a heavy-tailed distribution (1+Poisson⁡(λ)1+\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda) with log-normal λ\lambda, mean 12, cap 48; 9) and iterations past d/cd/c keep zdz_{d}. Forced depth is our default (PAR); §5.3 removes its need to know dd at test time.

3.3 Keeping the step map stationary

Extrapolation applies the step map hundreds of times, far beyond the training depths, so anything that drifts with kk or with absolute position eventually changes what the map computes. We remove two such drifts. State-norm anchoring rescales every token’s state to the RMS norm of its first-iteration state after each iteration (Figure 2a), sk←sk⋅rms⁡(s1)/rms⁡(sk)s_{k}\leftarrow s_{k}\cdot\operatorname{rms}(s_{1})/\operatorname{rms}(s_{k}), with a stop-gradient on the reference; R=1R=1 is unchanged. Positional stretch addresses long prompts, in which the query lies far from early moves: during a short fine-tuning stage we multiply position indices by s∼U⁡[1,smax]s\sim U[1,s_{\max}], ramping smaxs_{\max} from 1 to 8 [24, cf.], and test with ordinary positions. Label-supervised PAR reaches 16×16\times without the stretch; the label-free variant did not reach 16×16\times until fine-tuned with it (§6.3).

3.4 Reading completion: learned halting

Under the correspondence, whether the computation has finished is a property of the iteration index and the problem, so it can be supervised. As illustrated in Figure 2d, the coda read-out that produces the answer is also trained to put probability on the token Yes when c​k≥dck\geq d and on No otherwise, using class-balanced cross-entropy with weight 0.5 on every supervised iteration plus one earlier iteration as an extra negative. No parameters are added, and training never runs an iteration beyond dd. At test time we select the first answer iteration RR with P⁡(Yes)>τP(\texttt{Yes})>\tau such that at least kk of the iterations R,…,R+m−1R,\dots,R+m-1 also exceed τ\tau. After checking this confirmation window, we return the prediction made at RR. We use τ=0.5\tau=0.5, k=6k=6, m=8m=8; §6.2 explains how this rule was chosen.

3.5 Correspondence without step labels: prefix self-distillation

Intermediate answers zjz_{j} come for free from a synthetic generator but not from most real data. The correspondence supplies them anyway: the first jj steps of a problem form a shorter problem whose answer is zjz_{j}, and shorter problems are the ones a model learns first. As shown in Figure 2c, prefix self-distillation therefore uses only final answers. Iterations k≥⌈d/c⌉k\geq\lceil d/c\rceil receive cross-entropy on zdz_{d}. For each example, up to nkn_{k} earlier iterations k<⌈d/c⌉k<\lceil d/c\rceil are trained to match, by KL divergence, the answer distribution of a teacher that reads the same prompt truncated after c​kck steps, decoded at its own completion iteration. The teacher is an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student [31] or the live student.

3.6 Training

We use AdamW with learning rate 2×10−52{\times}10^{-5} (10−410^{-4} for the adapter), 200 warm-up steps and one epoch over ≈400{\approx}400k examples spread uniformly over training depths (compute details in Appendix A). No intermediate tokens are generated at training or test time.

4 Experimental Setup

Tasks. Group word problems. A prompt lists dd moves on five boxes, each holding a distinct item, and queries a box. In swap-S5S_{5} each move is the identity or one of the 10 transpositions; in A5A_{5} each move is a 3-cycle. Chance accuracy per query is 0.20.2. Swap-S5S_{5} protocol [11, 41]: we train on at most 32 moves and test on 1,0241{,}024 sequences per length. A sequence counts as correct only if all five boxes are answered correctly (full-state accuracy). Benchmarks from prior literature: the rule-table chain of Shapiro [28] (unary depth, train ≤8\leq 8, test to 64) and the graph reachability task of Chen [4] (train ≤5\leq 5 hops, test to 24).

Metrics. Accuracy is reported in % unless stated otherwise. On S5S_{5} and A5A_{5} we also report the extrapolation factor G=d50/dtrainG=d_{50}/d_{\text{train}}, where d50d_{50} is the first test depth at which accuracy with R=dR=d iterations falls below the midpoint between chance and 100%. With test depths up to 256 and dtrain=16d_{\text{train}}=16, G=16G=16 is the largest measurable value.

Baselines. With the same retrofitted Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone, data and step budget as PAR, we compare explicit CoT fine-tuning that writes the full state trace, a fixed-depth model (R=1R=1), an untied model with the core repeated four times (48 layers), and random-RR recurrence with state-norm [9]. On the swap-S5S_{5} protocol we also compare with Transformer and RLT, using the values reported by Zhang et al. [41] for their best split, 4+44+4 (mean over 3 seeds). Variants of PAR that remove one of its components, including the supervision schemes of prior work, are studied separately in §6.

5 Main Results

5.1 Depth extrapolation

Table 1 compares PAR with the baselines. On the swap-S5S_{5} protocol, PAR maintains over 95% full-state accuracy out to 16×16\times extrapolation, where RLT drops to 55.7% and every PAR seed exceeds RLT’s mean. On S5S_{5} and A5A_{5}, PAR achieves the maximum measurable extrapolation factor (G=16G=16) across all seeds, whereas fixed-depth, recurrent, and 48-layer untied baselines stay below 2×2\times: neither iteration count nor parameter count alone substitutes for the correspondence. Explicit CoT is perfect within the training range but collapses to chance by 8×8\times on swap-S5S_{5}, demonstrating that the pretrained backbone does not inherently confer extrapolation.

5.2 Larger and different backbones

Table 2 evaluates larger Qwen2.5 backbones (1.5B, 3B, and 7B) on S5S_{5}. On every backbone, the best PAR seed maintains 100% accuracy through d=256d=256, whereas fixed-depth baselines remain near chance (≤26.5%\leq 26.5\%). Across seeds, PAR provides substantial gains at all model sizes, with non-extrapolating seeds accounting for cross-seed variance.

Table 3 reports results on the Qwen3 family [40] across 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B scales. PAR consistently outperforms fixed depth across all evaluated depths: accuracy remains near ceiling at 2×2\times and maintains a wide margin through 8×8\times. At the 16×16\times horizon (d=256d=256), where fixed-depth models collapse near chance, PAR reaches up to 53% mean accuracy on 4B, retaining an advantage across scales despite increased seed variance on larger models.

5.3 Learning when to stop

Forced-depth models answer correctly at R=LR=L but degrade rapidly thereafter, dropping to near-zero accuracy within a few extra iterations at 16×16\times. Inference therefore requires identifying when execution finishes. With the “6 of 8” rule (§3.4), the jointly trained read-out halts without knowing problem length LL (Table 4): accuracy closely matches the oracle iteration count across all seeds and reaches 92.9%92.9\% at 16×16\times (vs. 55.7%55.7\% for RLT).

This stopping mechanism succeeds because jointly trained models enter a persistent finished state (Figure 3a), with P⁡(Yes)P(\texttt{Yes}) jumping from near zero before LL to near 1 afterwards. Because the answer representation itself remains valid for only a few steps past completion (Figure 3b), the rule reliably reads the prediction from the onset of the finished signal.

5.4 Learning without step labels

Prefix self-distillation learns the correspondence from final answers alone. Among the label-free models in Table 5, it is the only approach sustaining high accuracy at 16×16\times (85% at d=256d=256, G≥16G\geq 16), whereas alternative final-answer supervision recipes degrade substantially. While label-supervised PAR remains stronger at the longest depths (Figure 1b), positional stretch fine-tuning (§6.3) enables strong extrapolation on swap-S5S_{5}: fine-tuned models reach up to 99.7% accuracy at 16×16\times (Table 12), surpassing RLT without requiring step labels.

5.5 Prior benchmarks and scope

Benchmarks from prior literature. Table 6 evaluates the recipes on the benchmark tasks on which the final-answer and unanchored recipes were introduced. On the rule-table chain, an inherently sequential lookup problem, PAR-hold reaches G≥8G\geq 8 (94% accuracy at depth 64) and PAR reaches 6.0, whereas prefix targets without norm anchoring stall at 1.78.

Inductive bias and task structure. Graph reachability is solved by expanding a frontier in parallel rather than by a fixed sequence of steps, so it has no canonical intermediate state for iteration kk to hold; all recipes stay below 3.5×3.5\times on it. The correspondence targets sequential multi-step computation, the regime in which fixed-depth transformers fail [19, 21].

Natural-language format. On a BIG-Bench-Hard-style [29] tracking shuffled objects format with natural-language swaps, trained on ≤16\leq 16 swaps, PAR-hold with positional stretch reaches 94–96% at 32 and 79% at 64 swaps (chance 17%), whereas random-RR and fixed-depth baselines with the same stretch reach at most 67% and 21%. The original BBH items (3, 5 and 7 objects) lie within the training range, and all models score 95–100% on them.

6 Ablation Studies

6.1 Both conditions are necessary

Table 7 varies one condition at a time on S5S_{5} with training depth ≤16\leq 16. Three findings follow.

Final-answer targets do not define an iteration. Supervising zdz_{d} at every iteration stalls at G≈2G\approx 2, in line with Chen [4], while supervising it only at iteration dd reaches G=1.48G=1.48. Adding norm anchoring to iteration-dd supervision extends extrapolation for a single seed (G=8G=8), but the remaining seeds degrade earlier; across seeds, accuracy at depth 256 averages 26.8%, far below the near-perfect accuracy maintained by PAR.

The correspondence needs a stationary step map. Prefix targets without norm anchoring stall at ∼1.8×{\sim}1.8\times under either schedule, consistent with findings in unanchored recurrence [28], as state representations drift when iterated repeatedly.

Together, the two conditions extrapolate at least 16×16\times. PAR reaches G=16G=16 across all seeds with near-ceiling accuracy at d=256d=256. PAR-hold also extrapolates beyond 12×12\times, though with lower consistency across seeds.

Positional stretch alone does not create the correspondence. Applied as a fine-tune to the fixed-depth and random-RR models, positional stretch leaves both at chance by depth 48 (23% and 18%; Table 10). Applied to a PAR-hold model with step size c=2c=2, which already has the correspondence, the same fine-tune keeps 99% accuracy at depth 512, 32×32\times the training depth, in one run with a fixed R=288R=288. Stationarity makes an existing step map reusable; it does not create one.

A one-pass initialisation blocks the correspondence. On A5A_{5}, PAR trained from the pretrained parent reaches G=16G=16 on both seeds (Table 1). Warm-starting all layers from a fixed-depth model that already solves d≤16d\leq 16 in a single pass gives G≈1.4G\approx 1.4: the model keeps its one-pass solution and never learns the step map. Warm-starting only the prelude succeeds on one of two seeds.

6.2 Stopping rule and alternatives to halting

Stopping rule. Evaluating P⁡(Yes)P(\texttt{Yes}) at a single iteration is brittle (Table 8), as transient probability spikes cause premature stopping at long horizons. Conversely, requiring all 8 consecutive iterations to confirm completion is overly strict when probabilities fluctuate, delaying stopping until predictions drift. The “6 of 8” rule balances robustness and responsiveness, matching oracle stopping within 1.6 points across all evaluated sequences.

Joint training versus a fine-tuned read-out. Adding the read-out by fine-tuning an existing PAR checkpoint yields different dynamics (Figure 3a): P⁡(Yes)P(\texttt{Yes}) spikes sharply at completion and decays within two iterations. As a result, multi-step confirmation windows fail to trigger, whereas single-iteration stopping recovers oracle accuracy across both seeds (Table 11). However, fine-tuning causes minor accuracy degradation on one seed at 16×16\times compared to joint training.

Training on extra iterations is not a substitute. An alternative to an explicit halting signal is making completion an absorbing state by training models on extra iterations that must retain zdz_{d}. While this preserves in-distribution accuracy, it severely harms extrapolation: accuracy collapses below 1% at 16×16\times across evaluated seeds. Asking the recurrent core to advance intermediate states while simultaneously acting as a fixed point introduces conflicting objectives; an independent completion read-out avoids this competition.

6.3 Teacher and positional stretch in prefix self-distillation

Teacher. Three of five teacher configurations reach G≈16G\approx 16 or more (Table 9); the live-student teacher with a depth curriculum keeps the highest accuracy at d=256d=256.

Positional stretch. On swap-S5S_{5}, initial label-free models extrapolate partially to 8×8\times but collapse at 16×16\times (Table 12). The failure is abrupt rather than cumulative: per-query accuracy stays high at 256 moves before dropping to chance at 512, pointing to a non-stationary step map driven by absolute position encodings. A short fine-tune combining the label-free objective with positional stretch restores extrapolation across all starting checkpoints, raising 16×16\times accuracy from near-chance levels up to 99.7%. Training with stretch from the start similarly yields runs achieving perfect accuracy at both lengths, while label-supervised PAR achieves its results without stretch.

7 Conclusion

A looped language model extrapolates in depth when each of its iterations has a defined job. Aligning iteration kk with the first kk steps of the problem, and keeping the step map stationary, turns extra iterations into extra reasoning. A retrofitted 0.5B model trained this way surpasses the best published latent-recurrence model on swap-S5S_{5} at 8×8\times and 16×16\times the training length. The same correspondence lets the model learn when to stop and lets it learn its intermediate states from final answers alone. Defining what an iteration means is thus a training target in its own right, alongside choosing how many iterations to run.

Limitations

We evaluate on algorithmic and templated state-tracking tasks, where intermediate states are well defined; applying the correspondence to open-ended natural-language reasoning [39, 37, 36] is left to future work. Tasks without a sequential decomposition, such as graph reachability, fall outside its scope. Our scaling study covers Qwen2.5 backbones up to 7B and Qwen3 backbones up to 4B, with three seeds each, in the single-query S5S_{5} setting only; swap-S5S_{5}, learned halting and prefix self-distillation are evaluated only on Qwen2.5-0.5B. On the larger backbones, as with prefix self-distillation, results vary across seeds far more than for PAR on Qwen2.5-0.5B (standard deviations of 33–43 points at 16×16\times on Qwen2.5-1.5B to 7B), accuracy does not rise monotonically with Qwen2.5 size, and no Qwen3 backbone approaches Qwen2.5-0.5B at 16×16\times. These results therefore do not establish a monotonic trend with model size; characterizing the mechanisms of seed variance on larger backbones and stabilizing recurrent scaling remain open questions for future work.

Ethics Statement

This work studies training methods on synthetic reasoning tasks with publicly available models [14, 40]. It involves no human subjects and no personal data. Latent reasoning writes no intermediate steps, which makes it less transparent than chain of thought. Under the correspondence, however, every iteration can be decoded into the intermediate answer it holds, which offers a way to inspect the latent computation.

Appendix A Additional Results

Per-depth S5S_{5} results for the first recipe version. Table 10 gives accuracy by test depth for PAR-hold and the baselines (train d≤16d\leq 16).

PAR-hold on the swap-S5S_{5} protocol. Across 6 seeds evaluated on 1,024 sequences per length, PAR-hold with positional stretch achieves 84.5±29.4%84.5\pm 29.4\% at 8×8\times and 76.9±38.0%76.9\pm 38.0\% at 16×16\times, trailing forced-depth PAR in both mean accuracy and cross-seed consistency.

Explicit CoT by length. On the swap-S5S_{5} protocol, the explicit CoT baseline achieves perfect accuracy at the trained length (100% at 32 moves) but collapses rapidly beyond it: full-state accuracy drops to 35.6% at 64 moves, 3.1% at 128 moves, and collapses to 0.8% at 256 and 512 moves. Similarly, on the single-query S5S_{5} task (trained on depth ≤16\leq 16), CoT accuracy falls from 100% at depth 16 to 12% at 32, 4% at 64, and 0% at 128.

Per-seed halting results. Table 11 lists the per-seed results behind Tables 4 and 8.

Per-run label-free results on swap-S5S_{5}. Table 12 reports prefix self-distillation results on the swap-S5S_{5} protocol, before and after the positional-stretch fine-tune.

Compute. All runs train in bf16 with DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 [23], on two RTX 4090 or 3090 GPUs for Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen3-0.6B and on eight H200 GPUs for Qwen2.5-1.5B, 3B, 7B, and Qwen3-1.7B and 4B.

Configurations of the halting and label-free runs. Learned halting is trained jointly from the pretrained parent for one epoch with weight 0.5. The fine-tuned variant starts from two PAR checkpoints and trains for 0.3 epochs with learning rate 10−510^{-5}. The label-free models use forced depth, an EMA teacher with decay 0.99 read at its own completion iteration, and nk∈{2,4}n_{k}\in\{2,4\} distilled iterations per example, trained for 0.6 and 1 epoch. The positional-stretch fine-tune continues each starting model for 0.5 epochs with the same loss and nkn_{k} (step-6000 checkpoint for seed 2, step 5000 for seeds 4 and 5, final model for the nk=2n_{k}{=}2 seed 0). The stretch-from-the-start models train for one epoch with nk=2n_{k}{=}2.
